To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the growth of Gpi-anchored protein (Gpiap)-deficient progenitor cells is superior in vitro and that the in vitro growth of Gpiap-deficient progenitor cell is due to a higher rate of apoptosis of Gpiap-normal progenitor cells in vivo.

the higher apoptotic rates of normal progenitors in vivo result in a greater number of GPl-deficient cells in the bone marrow and that the higher number of GPl(-) progenitors results in a greater number that can be expanded in vitro.

the growth rate of progenitor cells deficient in GPI-APs is higher in vitro than in vivo and that this higher in vitro growth rate is due to the fact that progenitors with normal GPI-APs have a higher apoptotic rate in vivo than in vitro.

we have shown that GPIAPs are not required for normal hematopoiesis in the mouse.
